utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today the opening of the Defence case has been scheduled. As announced by Defence counsel, an opening statement will be made. At the same time, the Chamber still owes you a decision on the Zvornik contextual documents. That decision, and I already can inform the parties, that for 98 or 99 per cent the exhibits will be admitted. There is one or two items we just need perhaps a couple of days. So it's just about one or two contextual documents that there can be any doubt as to non-admission -- to admission or non-admission. Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to make its delayed opening statement under Rule 84?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, delayed opening statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Delayed; it's for you to choose whether you make your statement at the beginning of the case, at the beginning of the Defence case. To that extent I'm saying delayed opening statement. I had nothing more in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just wanted to be sure Your Honour. The word has cropped from time to time. May I start, please, Your Honours with just a reference to a cultural difference so there is no confusion. There is a cultural difference between the Prosecution team and the Defence team in this respect: That they -- many of them, and certainly the leading members of the Prosecution team, have practised for many years in the United States. The two counsel currently on the Defence team -- when I say "currently" I don't wish that to sound like "current wife." We intend to be on the team until the end of the case. But we have practised for many years at the Bar of England and Wales, and Mr. Josse's predecessor also practised in a common law system closer to the English system, in Australia. I say it for this reason, Your Honour: That there is a habit which is very different; that counsel from the United States will very often say they think something, that their opinion is something, and so on, and it's woven into their submissions in a way which, for us from a modest sized island off to the West of here, sometimes find difficult to disentangle. When we make submissions, Your Honour, we make submissions. We do not express personal opinions. It doesn't mean we don't have any. We're not intellectual units. We're not emotional units. Of course we do have our private opinions and sometimes our private opinions will coincide with the submissions. Sometimes they don't. Sometimes, of course, it may be fairly apparent, but that's another matter. That's, in a sense, behind the veil. Everything we say to the Court, apart if I say I think the air-conditioning is a bit fierce this morning, that's a personal opinion, that's not a submission, but leave aside that sort of thing. Everything we say to the Court is a submission. It is a submission as counsel for Mr. Krajisnik. It is the Defence case. It is Mr. Krajisnik's case. We are only - and I stress only - we are only Mr. Krajisnik's advocates. Mr. Krajisnik is on trial. We are Mr. Krajisnik when we stand up and make these submissions to the Tribunal. I am Mr. Krajisnik for these purposes. Mr. Josse is Mr. Krajisnik for these purposes. We do that -- the difference between us and Mr. Krajisnik is we are professional advocates and everything we do has to be consistent with our duties as members of our Bar and our duties as members of the association and our duties to this Tribunal in the way that we recognise duties to the Court on the basis of long practice in England and Wales. So, Your Honour, that preface, we submit, is important to understand the way in which we frame our submissions throughout this case and the way in which we present our case. Your Honour, there is - and it is absolutely unreal to suggest anything different - there is in relation to many cases before this Tribunal, and this one is no exception, a very high degree of prejudgement in the world outside this Court. When one puts forward names such as Karadzic - and I mean no disrespect to anybody today if I don't say Misters and Doctors and so on, it's just quicker to do it that way. When we put forward names of Karadzic, Mladic, Krajisnik we have here in Court, in the world outside many, many people have the clearest idea that these are just guilty men who just have to be got here in two of the cases that I have mentioned, and when they are got here, there will be a trial and then they will be convicted. Now, in a different part of the world, Saddam Hussein is on trial. It would be again unreal to suppose that in the world outside there is not a vast number of people who suppose that whatever trial Saddam Hussein obtains, the chances of his not being convicted at the end of the trial are simply zero. And one can imagine -- I obviously hold no brief one way or the other in relation to that matter, but one can imagine the political repercussions of an acquittal of a man whose actions supposedly are at the root of massive military action in that part of the world. I say this, Your Honours, because a very high degree of judicial courage is needed in relation to this sort of a case. This is one area where a bench of professional Judges is in some ways under greater pressure than a jury. A jury can largely retire after the case is over into relative obscurity and anonymity. It is a good thing if they do, on the whole. Any disagreements or objections to their verdicts may come, of course, from friends, relatives, acquaintances, and if I'm allowed to be a little bit English here, the chap you meet in the pub for a short time, and probably for a short time a jury member in a high profile case where a defendant is acquitted in circumstances where the media momentum has suggested very clearly to the populace at large that this is plainly a guilty man, terrible things have been done, it's supposed. Well, the police arrested him, no smoke without fire; all those matters with which anybody involved in the legal system is extremely familiar. Short-lived. It will have little or no effect, usually, on anybody's personal or professional reputation. It holds no real fears for an ordinary member of the public as a member of a jury. But the Judges of this Tribunal, with Your Honours' vast experience in the law and great skills that you bring to bear on this case, are in a different position because you inevitably can expect, must expect, and do expect, rightly, that your decisions, and your judicial reputations, of course, because just as barristers are only as good as their last case, there's a sense in which Judges' reputations are only as good as their last judgement, can expect your decisions and reputations to be under the closest scrutiny. And informed scrutiny. They will be subject to uninformed scrutiny, that just goes with the territory. Everybody involved in this matter. It's right. It's part of the public nature of a trial. It's not a disparagement. We don't expect the world to -- every person out there to live and breathe cases of this nature. It would be rather unfortunate for human life if they did. But an interest is important in the world at large, and scrutiny by what one might loosely call the informed public, and the informed international public, is something to which everything that happens in this Tribunal will be subjected. So -- and that will apply particularly forcefully if, as the Defence say, it should be and ultimately will be, if your verdict turns out to be something quite different from what the world at large and the legal and political community have been expecting. And we do put it in those terms because we don't wish this case to proceed in some utterly unreal vacuum. I will come to the question of how this case must proceed within the confines of a public court, within the confines of the evidence and so on. I'll come to that. But it is unreal to suppose that there aren't enormous pressures. And Your Honours, we're not submitting that Judges -- it would be an insolent submission to suggest that Judges of this Tribunal are not equipped and ready to withstand such pressures, but they are there. And this case, a case of this nature, and specifically Mr. Krajisnik's case, are at the top end of the scale of cases which require that degree of judicial courage to reach a decision which it is plain would not be the expected, and in many quarters would not be the desired result. Acquittal of Mr. Krajisnik would cause consternation. We know that, and Your Honours know that. But if it is the right result in the long term, not so much the consternation but the deep undermining of a judicial system if it is the wrong result, is -- far outweighs any such consternation. The -- it's a search for the truth. It is a search for the truth in an inevitably qualified way because, for a start, it's not divine justice. It's human justice. Divine justice, no personal opinions are going to be expressed in that area, but if divine justice has to be faced, that will be some other day, and that is not our direct concern. The search for the truth in this human system of justice is a search conducted in different ways by different systems, and Your Honours, along with your fellow Judges in this Tribunal, are constantly searching, we hope with the helpful assistance of counsel in this case as in other cases, for a reconciliation of the different cultures and the different systems, and many times in the course of this case Your Honours have correctly referred to the hybrid nature of the system under which this Tribunal operates. And, Your Honour, we unreservedly accept that it is that. We have had, and no doubt during the course of the rest of this case we will continue to have, submissions and debates, debates in a proper courtroom way about the balance and about what features should go into a hybrid system from different systems, starting from the position the Defence will always submit that the essential nature of these trials, as enshrined in the Statute and the Rules of Procedure, is adversarial. That, we submit, is plain whatever adjustments and qualifications are made. But whatever the balance of different systems, an essential feature of all criminal trials under any recognisably acceptable system is -- is this: That it is an individual on trial. And that is especially, especially a signal feature of the new International Criminal Court, with all the immunities swept away as a corollary effect. Precisely because it is individuals that are put on trial, individuals should not be able to escape liability, because if there is a human being in the dock, to use that phrase, who is on trial, then that human being, he or she, is not allowed to escape liability by saying, "Well, I was really my country. I was really my government. I was really only that." It is individual responsibility. But the other and most important and long established fundamental feature of any acceptable criminal system is that, as we know, there is not collective guilt. There must not be collective guilt. There must not be guilt by association. There must not be -- and it's not a technical phrase but I suggest that it's clear what we are saying; there mustn't be guilt by substitution. It must be that particular -- if there is to be a conviction ultimately, contrary to the Defence's submissions, it must be on the basis that that individual, and in this case it's Mr. Krajisnik, is himself criminally responsible for acts which are, of course, then by definition must be crimes. And in the very broadest terms, it means there must be justice, not vengeance. Again, we know, and there can't be any possible dispute, the idea that all is at peace -- all is at peace in the very clear, simple way in the former Yugoslavia, but the idea that all is at peace and all is sweetness and light and harmony and there is forgiveness, it is -- of course it isn't forgotten, we know that. Things don't get forgotten and they certainly are no more easily forgotten in the former Yugoslavia than in any other part of the world. That has become apparent in the course of this case. There are, not surprisingly, tremendously strong feelings. Anybody who, as many people have, lost family members in terrible circumstances, are going to harbour those feelings and they're going to harbour them for the rest of their lives. There is burning resentment among Serbs at many of the terrible things that were done by Muslims and Croats. There is burning resentment - resentment is too mild a word in the Muslim Community - at terrible things. And terrible things were done to the Muslims at terrible things were done to Muslims at the hands of Serb. It's no part of Mr. Krajisnik's case that that didn't happen. It would be unreal. Mr. Krajisnik does not wish to put forward any such absurd contention. But the state in a domestic prosecution, the international community, the combination of states which is behind this Tribunal and these prosecutions, and the Prosecution because the Prosecution is presenting the case against Mr. Krajisnik on their behalf, in effect, with the Trial Chamber having - and Appeals Chamber, if it should come to it - having the ultimate responsibility of the decision. But the Prosecution always have the burden, which the Trial Chamber, of course, and we don't suggest they would ever do anything different, loyally accept and apply the burden that to convict a human being of any crime - it applies even to trivial crimes, but we certainly don't have trivial crimes on the indictment in this case - to hold Mr. Krajisnik in this case individually responsible for these terrible events - and they were - to take away his freedom - now his freedom has been taken away the last few years anyway, but I'm talking about taking away his freedom at the end of this trial if he is convicted - requires proof by evidence. And the truth, tying in with the phrase the search for the truth, the truth, and it's the only truth which can be reached and found in this case, is the truth of what is established by the evidence. For the purposes of this trial and the purposes of the verdict against Mr. Krajisnik, that is the only truth. If there is any doubt, if there is any uncertainty, if there are any gaps, they must not be resolved or filled by speculation or guesswork. They can only be filled, if there are gaps, the case against Mr. Krajisnik can only be made and in the end he can only be convicted on evidence in this courtroom, within the ambit of admissible evidence. Of course it includes procedurally all the 92 bis evidence. Every bit of evidence is evidence, of course, but tautologically, everything which is not evidence is absolutely not evidence, apart from the obvious facts in the world of which judicial notice can be taken. The sun comes up in the east. We know that. Of course that's all part of evidence in a case, without getting into some academic analysis of it. That is well understood. But it's also well understood that beyond evidence in the case is, for the purposes of Mr. Krajisnik's guilt or innocence, a void. It just does not exist. Anything else of which one can't simply take judicial notice as to context of the world in which the evidence is presented, everything else is a void. There are different ways of expressing the burden of proof. Traditional English expression adopted and followed throughout the common law world has been for decades, centuries probably, Mr. Josse probably knows better than I do, he'll fill me in the on the history, but for centuries, I have some confidence in suggesting, that was beyond reasonable doubt. It's -- it's fallen into disuse a bit. The modern phrase adopted by criminal courts in England is for the Judge to tell the jury, because serious cases still are dealt with by juries, is for the Judge to tell the jury that you must be satisfied so you are sure that the defendant is guilty. The modern phrase is thought, and we're not quarreling with that, and we accept it anyway within our system, is thought to be clearer and more understandable to a jury, but in substance they're the same. Nothing in the Statute, Rules, or jurisprudence of this Tribunal even hints at any different test or standard, and we approach the case on the footing that this Trial Chamber would never be seeking to apply anything, however it was precisely phrased in words, never be seeking to apply any lower test or standard in Mr. Krajisnik's case. So the Defence are content, of course, with the test that before you can convict Mr. Krajisnik on any count, and there are a number of counts and each one, although they may overlap, each one has to be carefully and separately considered, and each of those counts you must be satisfied so you are sure that he is guilty. So any doubt which makes you feel unsure in relation to any count means that you must, and it's not -- I say must not in the sense it's our function to give orders to the Trial Chamber. Again, we would not be so insolent or presumptuous, but in terms of the duties that Your Honours have, you must then acquit Mr. Krajisnik. So far we only have the Prosecution evidence, of course. We are at this watershed now where we're coming to the Defence case. Your Honours have so far issued a decision that there is a case to answer, reached by clear indication, or expressed by clear indication by the rejection of the Defence's 98 bis application, which for those that don't pore over the Rules of this Tribunal, was our submission that on the Prosecution case evidence, there was no case to answer, that there was not sufficient evidence, without the Defence having to call any evidence, not sufficient evidence on which safely to convict Mr. Krajisnik. Now, Your Honours have rejected that, and I am not going to go into the -- all the appeal issues and the procedural matters of where we are, the tangle there in relation to appeal. Your Honours' decision is effectively this: That on all the evidence presented by the Prosecution, this Court has at this point decided that it would be possible that when that evidence is scrutinised, Mr. Krajisnik could be found guilty. It's not a finding that if Defence didn't call any evidence Mr. Krajisnik would, therefore, be convicted. The evidence would still have to be scrutinised if - which is not going to happen - if we didn't call a jot or an iota of Defence evidence. So the decision as it stands at the moment is not that he would be convicted and not that the evidence so far shows beyond reasonable doubt that he's guilty of anything. The decisions on those questions lie in the future. It's important for this reason, because it ties in with what we've already said this morning on the fundamental burden of proof. The Defence doesn't have to disprove the Prosecution case. In practice, as a factual matter, as a matter of presentation, the Defence case will include elements which will disprove aspects of the Prosecution case. The fact that you don't have to doesn't mean you don't do that where the Defence has evidence which does, in some cases - and we do submit this - in some cases will demolish the Prosecution evidence and in other cases will cast serious doubt on it, then we will present that evidence. But the fact that the Defence goes factually and evidentially beyond the burden doesn't change the burden. The Defence, after all, can, consistent with the burden, call no evidence at all. That's not what we're going to do, and I'll come to it. Your Honours know already that a very important feature of the Defence case is that Mr. Krajisnik himself is going to give evidence, and I will come to that. So the case remains open. There has been, whatever privately occurs in Chambers and whatever work is done on papers, there has been and cannot have been so far -- I get my grammar mixed up. There has been no detailed consideration of the case against Mr. Krajisnik on its merits, and there can't be yet because the Defence has always made it clear that it would be presenting evidence. The case is just a long way from over. The case remains open, and Mr. Krajisnik still, as he has done throughout and for the last five years Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that he's been confined to the United Nations -- five and a half years now, to the United Nations Detention Unit in the Hague, Mr. Krajisnik still stands in the metaphorical sense, he's sitting behind me here, stands innocent until eventually it's decided after the judgement of this Trial Chamber, any Appeals Chamber that looks at the matter, that he's guilty on any of the counts, and unless and until such a finding of guilt has been reached following a fair trial in which he has had sufficient opportunity of meeting the Prosecution case, including presentation of his own Defence by evidence called for him. This case includes one major feature absent from many trials on serious criminal charges, and that applies to trials in domestic courts as well as international tribunals. Right from the outset of this trial and -- well, here I'm just expressing my personal recollection, Your Honours; my recollection is it was very early in the trial. Whether it was days or whether it was a tiny number of weeks, but very early indeed in the trial it was made clear by Mr. Krajisnik's lawyers, that was -- that's always included me since before the trial began, and on occasions when the opportunity has been given to him, by Mr. Krajisnik himself, that he would be giving evidence himself and would, therefore, and will therefore be subjecting himself to cross-examination on the huge range of issues put forward by the Prosecution as relevant to the case against Mr. Krajisnik. And, Your Honours, I again expressing just personal recollection here, I believe that at no point during this trial has Mr. Krajisnik, certainly not his lawyers on his behalf, has Mr. Krajisnik ever resiled from that position or ever expressed any contingent or provisional nature of his decision to give evidence. Clearly contingent if the Prosecution case had been dismissed on the 98 bis application, then of course he would have, but apart from that obvious point, Mr. Krajisnik's firm commitment has never been qualified in any way at all. Mr. Krajisnik remains firmly and unequivocally committed to doing what he has always wanted to do in this case and said he would do; to tell the true facts as he sees them - he can only present them as he sees them, like any human being, as he honestly sees them - and to explain as fully as possible, first in this instance by his own evidence but also more broadly by the evidence of other Defence witnesses, the truth as to what has happened. And Mr. Krajisnik has consistently expressed, and through me today as his advocate, expresses again the strong wish that the facts should be as thoroughly investigated as possible, and in particular that he, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, has the full opportunity of giving his personal account of the enormously wide-ranging events brought up by the Prosecution. At present, despite the considerable time that this trial has taken, and correctly taken because the events are so wide-ranging, at present the Trial Chamber of course has only a partial and incomplete picture of the relevant events. It will always be incomplete for the reasons I've recognised. This is not -- this is human justice. We can't recreate -- we're not out to recreate them, of course, but we can't simply draw the complete picture of what happened in former Yugoslavia in the early 1990s. That's not possible. A human court can only do its best, but the best can go a long way, and again, if the best does not produce a clear, undoubted compendium of evidence which shows unequivocally that the defendant is guilty, then he is not guilty and he remains innocent. But Mr. Krajisnik wishes and intends to present a full Defence. It's not his burden, but he will present a full Defence which will fill out the picture. It will explain misunderstandings, and it will remove misconceptions which could easily be gained from the Prosecution case. And it will lead to the conclusion not just that there is sufficient doubt, which is enough, but that conviction of Mr. Krajisnik would be a serious miscarriage of justice because it would be the conviction of an innocent man for the crimes of others. This isn't a case in which there have been no crimes. That's obvious. The Defence hasn't sought, except it sought to test, of course, and that's legitimate, from time to time, but in many instances - probably, on examination of the record and the transcript, most instances - the Defence has not sought to challenge the veracity of the evidence which has described appalling crimes committed against individuals in different parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially in 1992. That was an annus horribilis, there is no question about it. We heard -- I have to be careful because, without double-checking, I can't be 100 per cent sure whether the particular witness is a protected witness or not, but we heard a -- within the last two or three months of the Prosecution case, a woman described to the Trial Chamber how her children were snatched from her, never seen again, and they're dead. That's clear. Her husband is certainly dead, and his body, the remains of his body have been found. The Defence doesn't suggest that those things didn't happen. We don't suggest that that lady bravely -- that she didn't bravely come to tell the truth in relation to those matters. Of course she did. And nobody could suggest that her recollection of those events, except in the most irrelevant detail, could possibly be mistaken. People do invent things, but that lady was not inventing those things. That's not the Defence case. Those were terrible events and it's not the Defence case that they weren't and it didn't happen. The Defence case does include - but, Your Honours, we hope that we have and will continue to keep it properly within the confines of where it has a relevant bearing on Mr. Krajisnik's case - the Defence case does include that crimes were committed on all sides. Terrible crimes were committed on all sides. Proportions don't help the individuals. If there were three times as many of one nationality subjected to appalling brutality as another nationality, it's dismal arithmetic, and it's not arithmetic that the Defence wishes to explore in an unproductive and depressing way. Those things happened. Mr. Krajisnik doesn't defend himself and he won't defend himself and he refuses to defend himself by an irresponsible denial that terrible events and terrible crimes were committed in many parts of Bosnia, especially in the last year for which Mr. Krajisnik is indicted. Awful things have happened since as well, but Mr. Krajisnik is charged with the responsibility up to very near the end of 1992, and 1992 particularly was a year in which -- most of the terrible things of which Your Honours have heard evidence in this case happened in 1992, whatever their genesis. This was an appallingly brutal war, if there ever can be a war without brutality. There were killings, rapes, tortures, brutal ill-treatment on an appalling scale. There was devastating destruction of lives and property. There was ravaging of homes and livelihoods. Mothers, fathers, sons, daughters, brothers, sisters were lost by tens or hundreds of thousands. Nobody in their right mind denies that. So Mr. Krajisnik doesn't deny it. No nationality or group went unharmed and unscathed, and every nationality and every ethnic group both suffered and harboured and still harbours among their numbers war criminals. There was brutality on all sides. There is no excuse for -- there isn't an excuse for any of those terrible acts of brutality. The -- in wartime, there are, of course, the legitimate -- once a war has started, there are legitimate actions of self-defence or legitimate aggression in the course of the war once it's started. That's not what this case is about. After all, people don't just get put on trial for killing the enemy in the course of a war, tragic though that is in human terms. Only the most -- well, only the fortunate families in that region of the world escaped unscathed and unmarked by tragic loss. And as it happens, Mr. Krajisnik's own family was not among the fortunate. In the midst of all this turmoil, it's not -- I'm not putting it forward, it's not the central feature of the case, but it is a central feature of Mr. Krajisnik's life and Mr. Krajisnik is the man on trial. In the midst of all the turmoil and pain of that brutal year, in August 1992, Mr. Krajisnik lost his own wife and the mother of his three children. It was and is a large event in the life of Mr. Krajisnik and his own children. But notwithstanding that tragedy within Mr. Krajisnik's own family, if he were truly responsible in any way for these terrible crimes, then he would have to answer for them, in this world, wherever else, and before this Court. I say no more about that personal tragic event. Mr. Krajisnik will give his own account of the war from where he was and from what he knows, from what he saw, what he knew about, and the events which led up to it. But Mr. Krajisnik - and Your Honours will hear this and it is part of the picture - Mr. Krajisnik had a human family life as well in parallel to all his work and his political activities. You will, therefore, have the opportunity of judging the man. You're judging ultimately the responsibility of the man or not responsibility for the crimes with which he's charged, but you will have the opportunity of judging the man as well as part of Your Honours' heavy task in reaching your conclusions whether he is to be held criminally responsible in this Tribunal. Now, there are some questions in relation to Mr. Krajisnik, the man, which do have a significant bearing, must be taken into account in assessing his responsibility for any crimes. Are there inflammatory statements by Mr. Krajisnik, as - and we don't reject this label and Mr. Krajisnik doesn't reject the label of his being in some sense one of the Bosnian Serb leaders. It requires more careful analysis to see where it leads, but that as a simple label is not rejected and couldn't be rejected by the Defence. Are there inflammatory statements? The Prosecution point to and have pointed to a small number of passages of Mr. Krajisnik's public utterances that they would suggest fall into that category. I'm not getting into that this morning because -- not because it's -- they are to be avoided or evaded or not faced by the Defence, but the time to look at those in detail is going to be particularly when Mr. Krajisnik gives evidence, because that's his opportunity to explain whatever he was saying on whatever occasion and to be cross-examined on that. But are there -- are there racist remarks by Mr. Krajisnik? Are there offensive, abusive statements about members of other nationalities? Well, there aren't. There are plenty of those statements around on all sides. There are plenty such statements on record from that period on all sides, but Your Honours have seen the way in which Mr. Krajisnik conducted himself. Are there -- are there orders by Mr. Krajisnik to commit crimes or to do acts which were in fact crimes? If there aren't, that doesn't itself mean necessarily that he can't be convicted. We're not putting forward an unreal submission, but it's an important point. The Defence position on that is clear: No, there aren't. Are there directions, orders, instructions from Mr. Krajisnik to the army, to the police, to municipal leaders? Again, the Defence submission, based on the evidence is no, there aren't. So what is the case against Mr. Krajisnik? Not the case to be analysed. This is an opening statement. It's the -- nothing I say this morning will in the end have any real importance, weight, or significance if it turns out to have no connection with the evidence in this case, because we go back to the evidence. But as a -- we see the purpose of the opening statement as to just, at this important juncture in the case, just help if it does help in a small way, just help to achieve some -- some contribution to the direction, some clarity as to where this case is now supposed to go, and that's not intended in any presumptuous way in a Court where Your Honours have great experience, knowing where cases go anyway, but this particular case, what are the Prosecution essentially trying to do? It's all about links, isn't it? When there has been legitimate, not informal but legitimate exploration of this case and where it is going in procedural meetings and 65 ter conferences or in Court, we know that when the -- there's a crime base, and I've already said probably pretty much as much as the Defence would wish to say this morning about what we've called the crime base. These individual events, the violent events that took place throughout Bosnia, particularly from the end of March, beginning of April, then through the ensuing months of 1992. Of course there was violence and there were pockets of violence and there was arming and there were incidents before war broke out, but that's when it really started. Mr. Krajisnik can't and mustn't be convicted unless there is the link or there are the links that make him individually criminally responsible for those events. Now, he was a Bosnian Serb leader. Yes, he was. That's not -- that's not the link. That doesn't -- that's not the end of case. It would be a bit simple. All these events happen, Mr. Krajisnik is one of the Bosnian Serb leaders, therefore he's guilty. Nobody -- the Prosecution don't suggest - or we hope they don't and if they do it's just not good enough - don't suggest that that can be the basis of a conviction of Mr. Krajisnik. What were his leadership positions? Well, yes, he was throughout the whole of the relevant period, he was the president. In some other terminology from some other countries, that might be called the speaker. No two systems are exactly the same; he was the president, he was the speaker of the Serb Assembly. He had been, we know, an important figure in Bosnia and Herzegovina before the split, because he had been the same thing, the president and the speaker of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly, and he has already received, in the course of the Prosecution evidence, considerable plaudits for his work as the president of that Assembly. But, Your Honours, all the plaudits in the world for the efficiency and the effective handling and diplomatic handling of that particular task and that particular job, that doesn't mean somebody is guilty or innocent of crimes. We don't submit that. But as the speaker of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, we're not going to go into elaborate submissions this morning, but just going to pose the question: Does that normally -- I leave aside normally. Could that in this case constitute the link to make Mr. Krajisnik criminally liable for the actions and events of which evidence has been given? I'm just going to give you the short answer this morning, Your Honour. No. It's just not enough. That will be -- have to be elaborated in due course in a full final brief, if we ever get time to write one. But it raises the question, well, what beyond that? Because that's not enough. And we have seen from the Prosecution evidence that implicitly the Prosecution themselves or the Prosecution case recognises it can't be enough, because they've been trying throughout the Prosecution case to establish other links and other routes, other channels by which Mr. Krajisnik can be held responsible. And this is not the point in the case to argue the case in any full sense. This is the point in the case to raise the questions, to give the pointers, to indicate where the Defence say that there are real weaknesses and real gaps and real flaws in the Prosecution case. Expanded Presidency. I'm going to keep all these items short, but expanded Presidency. There are two aspects to that. One is the technical legal aspect, the de jure aspect. The other is the actual factual position, the de facto aspect. Your Honours already know from the examination and exploration of this aspect of the case during the Prosecution case that there is in the terms of the legal and constitutional system established as the Republika Srpska or by the Republika Srpska, if you like. That's the name that superseded at some point in early 1992 the Serb Republic, then Republika Srpska, the animal or the entity which emerged after the split in the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly in mid-October 1991, and then by January, certainly by the beginning of the war, had been established as a serious entity with its own constitutional legal documents, its own structure. There is and always was a flaw in the -- within Republika Srpska terms in the establishment of the expanded Presidency because the specific condition required to trigger off the expanded Presidency never in fact occurred. A state of war. There was a declaration of an imminent state of war, but strictly speaking, it never existed within those terms. However, that's not a -- that's not a trivial point, because so far as the Prosecution seek to pin liability on Mr. Krajisnik based on the technical legal status of the expanded Presidency and his membership of it, that just fails in terms. It's maybe a technical point in a sense, but it's a technical point, to me it's a technical point, if you like. It's a legal answer to a legal point, because the Defence doesn't suggest that you don't move on, then, straight away to the question of whether there was a body calling itself and perhaps believing it was the expanded Presidency, perhaps with an unrecognised flaw. That's something that just has to be considered on the evidence, an unrecognised flaw in its own constitution and its own legality within the Republika Srpska constitutional and legal system. When one looks at the expanded Presidency, yes, there are -- there are minutes, there are documents, there are agendas of some sort indicating a body, the expanded Presidency, but the evidence of Mr. Krajisnik's participation in that expanded Presidency and the evidence of what actual authority, what actual influence that body had over the events in question, and the evidence of any serious linkage between that body and Mr. Krajisnik personally and what happened is flimsy. It will require to be most carefully considered, and our submission at this point is just that it is flimsy. Another route through which the Prosecution seek to establish the link between Mr. Krajisnik himself and the crimes is through Mr. Karadzic. Now, Your Honours, we hold in a perfectly proper way the brief for Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik is our concern. Mr. Krajisnik is our client. Mr. Krajisnik's Defence is what we present. And we don't present any other Defence for anybody else. Neither do we present any prosecution of anybody else. We are not Dr. Karadzic's lawyers. We do not make any submissions in relation to Dr. Karadzic except, when the evidence is complete, so far as they have a genuine bearing on our client, Mr. Krajisnik's position and the case against him. If - Mrs. Del Ponte would prefer it to be described as when - Dr. Karadzic is apprehended, he will be put on trial and somebody else will have the responsibility of prosecuting him, and somebody else will have the responsibility of defending him, but it isn't us. The -- the Prosecution in this case against Mr. Krajisnik use as one of the routes, one of their attempts to construct a chain from Mr. Krajisnik to these events, they want to go through Dr. Karadzic. Now, of course they've got to establish sufficiently -- the Prosecution have got to establish sufficiently a direct link from Dr. Karadzic to those events, because otherwise a link between Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic doesn't help them anyway. But let's leave that aside, certainly for today, leave aside the link of Dr. Karadzic to events, just entirely on one side. Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Karadzic, they were put on trial together a few years ago. One might be forgiven for not understanding for quite a lot of Prosecution case that they were completely acquitted, and ultimately we had the Judge in that case, as it happens, in Court giving evidence and making it absolutely clear first that he really just didn't think there was anything like a case against them; and secondly, expressing the view, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which he's entitled to express, that there was some political motivation for the prosecution in the first place. That sort of evidence just needs to be thrown aside. Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic knew each other. That's neither a crime nor a sin nor a surprise. Mr. Krajisnik will explain and, Your Honours, we undertake to keep it as best we can within the proper confines of relevance, Mr. Krajisnik will explain, when he gives evidence, how he first came to know Dr. Karadzic, what their relationship was over the years they've known each other. After all, the Prosecution wish to make the relations between Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic an important feature of their case. So it's going to have to be an element of the evidence that Mr. Krajisnik himself gives to Your Honours. Mr. Krajisnik attended -- participated, didn't just attend. Mr. Krajisnik participated in a significant number of significant international negotiations in attempts, and laudable attempts by all concerned, to try to resolve the many and complicated conflicts in former Yugoslavia by as peaceful means as could be managed. That's a leadership role in some clear sense. Mr. Krajisnik, of course, participated in very important negotiations a considerable time after the indictment period, when he was at Dayton, but he was involved in the earlier negotiations which did take place in 1991, 1992, during the indictment period. The Bosnian Serbs, no less than anybody else, didn't send the tea boy to the negotiations, they sent their leaders, or, if you like, the people they sent to negotiations of that importance thereby become leaders. They become important because they send them. Dr. Koljevic was there frequently. Dr. Karadzic was nearly always there. Mr. Krajisnik was nearly always - very often - there at those negotiations. It's a not incidental, it's a slightly subsidiary point, that Dr. Karadzic and Dr. Koljevic and both, and this is clear on the evidence, both had a very good command of English. And in Dr. Koljevic's case, he could even go out in the corridors and discuss Shakespeare. Mr. Krajisnik had, and for practical purposes has, no useful English, so his participation in all these - with interpreters, of course - but his participation in all these discussions has to be judged in that light. I won't dwell on it, Your Honour. Mr. Krajisnik can describe in more detail how it went, but English speaking participants, and particularly when we're looking at the talks involving Mr. Cyrus Vance and Mr. Okun who came here, English speakers on one side of the table, English speakers, not native English speakers on the other side of the table or somewhere else on the table. It's Mr. Krajisnik's participation -- Your Honours, we aren't submitting -- we won't be submitting that Krajisnik wasn't a serious participant. We're not suggesting he was just some fly on the wall or some non-participant through the language issue. We're not going that far, we're just putting it in context. But when we consider -- and it's neither my task nor would it be useful today for me to start exploring the ins and outs of the evidence of the individual witness who have given evidence, but I've mentioned one earlier, not by name, a victim of terrible crimes, this is the second one I'm mentioning this morning -- well, I've mentioned not by name, it was Mr. Trbojevic. There's no secret about his identity either; the judge who dealt with the prosecution of Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic. I think this is now the third part while I'm mentioning Mr. Okun. Mr. Okun as Mr. Vance's deputy attended a number of meetings at which Mr. Krajisnik was present. He made extensive notes. He came and gave evidence before this Tribunal. Your Honour, Mr. Okun is a highly respected man with a distinguished career. What is important with a witness such as Mr. Okun is just to be careful about the limits of what he can say and what he is saying. He could only give -- in the end, he can give an account of any of the actual substance of the negotiations, but that wasn't really the issue. Your Honours are not here, and the Prosecution case doesn't really involve going into the ins and outs of those particular negotiations. Some of the other ones, the Cutileiro ones are another matter, but the detailed content and how the discussion progressed from one meeting to the next, from one hour to the next, don't really arise. The thrust of Mr. Okun's evidence was Mr. Krajisnik's influence over Dr. Karadzic. Mr. Krajisnik was there. When Mr. Krajisnik wasn't there, he was there in spirit. You can be somewhere in spirit, of course. It's just that it requires the utmost care if somebody's presence in spirit is presented as a significant ingredient in a criminal prosecution for the charges with which Mr. Krajisnik faces. That's where great care has to be taken. So Dr. Karadzic consulted Mr. Krajisnik. Dr. Karadzic took notice of what Mr. Krajisnik said. Dr. Karadzic listened to Mr. Krajisnik. It would be a bit odd if he didn't. The Bosnian Serbs want to send a group of people around Europe, and eventually around the world, to negotiations where one of them, Mr. Krajisnik, who was the president of their Assembly is just there as a piece of the furniture? Well, hardly. Of course Dr. Karadzic took some notice of Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik was there, apart from anything else, because there was an Assembly. There was a functioning parliament and we see it. It wasn't a tame animal throughout the period concerned. And certainly I don't mean animals, of course Your Honours don't misunderstand that, but the individual deputies were not -- we can see from the transcripts they weren't all household pets that just did what they were told and never squeaked up and argued about what was going on. Decisions and proposals and agreements had to be carried back to Republika Srpska, and they had to be referred to the Assembly. Now, we don't -- the Defence case does not -- not rest on Mr. Krajisnik being unimportant. That would be a ludicrous submission to make. Of course he wasn't unimportant. Why was he -- why was he there at these international negotiations? He was the president of the Assembly. But that's a different point. Being important doesn't make you criminally responsible. You have to look at what the man actually did. You can't just look at the positions. You can't look at just at whether he was there in spirit, can't even just look at whether he was respected, whether he was relied upon, whether he was consulted, whether he was viewed as important. All the time you have to look rigorously, what did he do? What did he say? What decisions did he participate in? What were his actual responsibilities? What were his powers? What was he able to get other people to do? What was he able to stop other people from doing? Those are the questions. Not just labels. We've had -- I'm not going to dwell on individual witnesses to any significant degree. I will mention one or two more in the course of the next hour or so, but we've had witnesses come along, we've had the Prosecution entering into -- they've got their job to do, Your Honour, but some of the evidence was like -- like watching a very -- well, a second team club tennis match, with the Prosecution asking a witness who knew no more than what he'd seen on television and could read in the newspapers, who were the important people in Republika Srpska, who were the important people in the power structure. And I do put this submission quite strongly in these terms, Your Honour. Some of this evidence is just like going out with a clipboard on the street and asking the first six people who come along to tell you who in their view are the important leaders. In England, they'd end up identifying band leaders as cabinet ministers. It's just -- some of the evidence is really, on that level really quite farcical, and Your Honours must, with respect, rigorously examine that evidence and toss out that sort of evidence. It's worthless. The case must focus on what Mr. Krajisnik actually provably and proven did and said. What are supposedly the links between Mr. Krajisnik and the army or the police? They've got to be shown. They've got to be scrutinised. They've got to be examined. Whatever label one attaches and whatever positions Mr. Krajisnik held -- National Security Council, not very much evidence of what that did, is there? Personnel commission. What on earth has that got to do with anything, once we've actually had a look at the evidence in the light of day? Look at what he actually did. What did Mr. Krajisnik in relation to the army? What's the link there between Mr. Krajisnik and the army? There was a General Staff. What -- what contacts, what control, what powers, what authority, what is shown for Mr. Krajisnik there? He had a conversation with Mr. Mladic. I don't remember the details. We're going to look at them. Not today, but in due course we'll look at them again, so I won't take the risk of misstating it because I don't remember it in detail. Has a conversation with Mr. Mladic in which it ends up with something like -- and we'll look at it in due course and it doesn't matter if I'm rather crudely paraphrasing it, it's something like, "Well, I'll come round in the morning then and you can tell me what to do." Something like that. Well, we're going to hear Mr. Krajisnik explain what he can remember about that, and what it did mean and what it could possibly mean. The same with the police. There's not much for me to say this morning on this because we -- we shall look at the evidence in due course, but even if we did look at the evidence, frankly, there wouldn't be much to say anyway because there isn't much evidence. Municipal authorities. All these 109 municipalities throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. We -- we get some evidence of Mr. Krajisnik visiting a particular municipality on a particular day. On a superficial view, it looks like a serious business meeting. It looks and is presented as if the Bosnian Serb leaders, in the guise of Mr. Krajisnik on that occasion, have gone to the municipality to start giving instructions about exactly how they're going to run their municipality and how they're going to deal with the existing or imminent conflict. The reality is that it's -- it's a special day. It's -- I can't remember. It's a saint's day, it's a festive day of some sort. I don't mean to diminish it or disparage it if I simply don't remember what the day was, but it was an important day in the Serb calendar. Mr. Krajisnik is clearly, even on the evidence as it stands at the moment without Mr. Krajisnik, as he will do, explaining to Your Honours what happened on such occasions, it's apparent that it was -- it was an invitation to, in this context, a dignitary. Mr. Krajisnik for these purposes can broadly be labelled with the rather pompous sounding English word, anyway, of dignitary. He was there for that purpose. And of course, courtesies and politeness require on such occasions that are some meetings and everybody is familiar with situations there where at least there's some sort of diplomatic presentation of something, it looks like some sort of business meeting, but there's no content, there's nothing shown by way of any real authority. But we don't see orders from Mr. Krajisnik. We don't see instructions. We don't see directions. We got all sorts of flimsy evidence about reports, but we don't see them, haven't -- practically nothing concrete going back to Mr. Krajisnik, only the flimsiest suggestions that he was in any way running or controlling or directing what was happening in these 109, in many cases far-flung, municipalities which in a number of instances for a considerable period that we're looking at were cut off anyway from where Mr. Krajisnik was. Communications cut off, hopeless to have any thought of controlling what those people were doing. And he's supposed to have been -- he's supposed to have been following closely and controlling and directing what was happening in the municipalities through his relations with the deputies in the Assembly. They are supposed to have been there in their municipalities soaking up and gathering the information, carrying it to Pale after April 1992, and before that, to Sarajevo, reporting it to Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik's "influence" over the deputies enabled him, then, to get them to carry back to the -- I'm certainly -- I'm exaggerating what has come out of the evidence, but in our submission I'm not exaggerating what the Prosecution would like and suggest that you should get out of that evidence, but you can't get it out of the evidence that Mr. Krajisnik -- so he has some influence over deputies. He would be a very poor president of the Republika Srpska Assembly if he had no influence over the deputies in his own parliament. He would get the sack in no time. It's a basic qualification of the job that you culcate some respect in the deputies of the parliament over which you're presiding, and the influence. We know what happens in parliaments. There is procedural wheeling and dealing going on all the time behind the scenes. That's apparent already without Mr. Krajisnik describing it in detail. Mr. Krajisnik, the evidence from Prosecution witnesses is clear; Mr. Krajisnik is A, good at that sort thing; B, likes doing it. On the whole, people are good at that sort of thing because they like doing it. If you don't like doing it, you're likely to be pretty hopeless. Mr. Krajisnik likes that sort of thing, and he's good at it, and he's efficient at it. And in the Bosnian Serb Assembly, as in any other parliament, there is timetabling. There is trying to get off the agenda issues which don't have to be contentious by getting them sorted out without having to bring them into the Chamber, and trying to cut down to minimum those matters which really require extensive debate. Now, I don't -- in a way it's not necessary, but it's not really proper for me to go any further because we've had such a limited and slight account from Prosecution witnesses as to what was really going on. On that point it could almost be left there because they don't cross the threshold of any sort of burden in that pocket of the case. But Your Honours are going to hear explanations and accounts of that. Your Honours are going to hear it from Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honours are going to hear that from deputies in the Republika Srpska Assembly. Your Honours are going to get a proper feel of what was actually happening and what Mr. Krajisnik was actually doing. Now, Your Honour -- Your Honours, I haven't finished there. I see it's twenty-five to eleven.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The -- Your Honours have heard quite a bit of evidence already about variants A and B and also another significant aspect of the Prosecution's evidence, there's been evidence in relation to six strategic goals. Those are clearly major items for exploration in the evidence and they will indeed be important items for consideration in the Defence evidence, and particularly in the evidence of Mr. Krajisnik. As far as Variants A and B are concerned, we will confine ourselves this morning to relatively brief comments. The evidence in relation to that variant A and B document is, on the Prosecution case as we have it now, to put it euphemistically, untidy. It is a very long way from showing that this was in any sense an official document of the SDS leadership which was part of some concerted and organised plan involving dissemination of such instructions to all the municipalities. Just even on the Prosecution evidence, it just doesn't come across like that at all. It's an extraordinary document -- without dwelling on the details, it's an extraordinary document with some extraordinary features just on its face if it really is what the Prosecution say it was. And even from the Prosecution witnesses we have seen the enormous disparities in the way in which that document did or didn't reach particular municipalities or particular municipality leaders, what was or wasn't done with it, whether they'd ever heard of it, what steps were taken, if any, in relation to that document, just on the Prosecution evidence alone, indicate that it is a very long way from being what the Prosecution say it is. One further comment to make on variants A and B is that it's of course been a document which has featured in other cases. Well, of course -- leave aside "of course," it has featured in other cases before this Tribunal. So far as evidence in other cases has become evidence in this case, well it's thrown into the whole melting pot of evidence in the case against Mr. Krajisnik. So far as any adjudicated facts or evidence introduced by way of 92 bis, so far as that has not happened, so far as such material and such consideration of variants A and B in other cases has not found its way into this case, it is in that void that I referred to earlier on. It absolutely must be disregarded. The relevance, significance, genesis, the importance of variants A and B are to be judged, and the application or non-application of that document is to be judged by Your Honours against Mr. Krajisnik or in favour of Mr. Krajisnik on the evidence in Mr. Krajisnik's case. And Your Honours will hear more about those matters during the course of evidence in the Defence case. So far as six strategic goals are concerned, I wouldn't begin to get into what is a large and complicated topic on the evidence simply to say that Your Honours will know already from the approach adopted by the Defence during the course of the Prosecution case that the Defence case and Mr. Krajisnik's position is that the six strategic goals, as a policy, in the context of the conflict and in the context of the concerns and fears that the Bosnian Serbs had, was not in any of its elements or overall in any way a criminal plan. It wasn't part of any criminal plan. It wasn't inherently criminal. And neither in any respect in which it was followed and implemented by the Bosnian Serb leadership was it criminal in any way from -- for which Mr. Krajisnik, on the evidence, can be said to have any responsibility. What happened on the ground in the fighting, in the conflict, nobody can -- on the fullest evidence, nobody can ever draw a clear defined line which shows what actions in what corners, in what quarters of Bosnia were or weren't conducted supposedly by the people who were carrying them out in implementation of some specific plan. It just never is as neat as that. But so far as the six strategic goals will be explored, do require careful scrutiny, Your Honours will hear from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Krajisnik himself what they were about, what he -- because of course he doesn't disclaim knowledge of the six strategic objectives. That would be an absurd contention. Of course he doesn't. Mr. Krajisnik attended the Cutileiro and was a participant in the Cutileiro talks, and there is a clear and close link between what was contemplated by the Lisbon and Sarajevo agreements reached as a result of the Cutileiro talks, but not, in the end, of course followed through because of changes of heart and changes of position particularly by Mr. Izetbegovic, the Bosnian Muslim leader. There are different views and different assessments of the Cutileiro plan itself and the Lisbon and Sarajevo agreements, but Your Honours are going to have a better, clearer, expanded picture of what was involved in the six strategic goals and how they tie in with the legitimate, positive, and entirely good faith efforts of the participants in the Cutileiro negotiations to try to achieve - unfortunately, didn't succeed - try to achieve a peaceful resolution of the disputes and burgeoning conflicts at that time. The quality of the Prosecution evidence, since the Defence are going to present a case and are going to present not just Mr. Krajisnik's evidence but the evidence of a substantial number of other witnesses, the quality of the Prosecution evidence is always, as in any case, of course an important consideration, and many criminal cases, again both in domestic jurisdictions and before this Tribunal, produce a range of Prosecution witnesses including in some cases the clearly criminal themselves among the array of Prosecution witnesses. We do have in this particular case the most extreme range of witnesses in relation both to their part, active or passive, in the events in question, or in some cases their limited participation in the actual events in Bosnia but their connection in some way with those events. We have extremes in the at least superficial reliability of their evidence. At one end of the spectrum we have, again, the lady that I mentioned earlier who -- she and her family were -- her family particularly and she herself in that very direct sense were absolute victims of this conflict. I take her, and it's intended as a positive, complimentary remark about that witness, I take her really as the paradigm of a genuine good faith, truthful, reliable witness where it would be absurd for the Defence to suggest there was any significant doubts about her evidence. If she has misremembered something, probably none of us and Your Honours would ever be able to see if she's misremembered something because it could only be on the most incidental and trivial aspects of her evidence. The essential thrust of what she -- and there are other witnesses in that category. It's not necessary or appropriate at the moment to identify them, but at some point the Defence would expect to make clear which of the Prosecution witnesses we regarded as being in that category or what areas we regarded as being in that category. It's already implicit in some of our responses on 92 bis applications and so on. That's one end of the spectrum. The other end of the spectrum, and I don't make the slightest apology for singling him out because, well, he deserves no more and no less; take somebody like Mr. Deronjic. I have no wish to, on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf, to make Mr. Deronjic's already no doubt very difficult life more difficult, but he is a despicable character. That has to be said. Mr. Deronjic murdered more than 60 people. He, with others, torched a village. People were burnt to death. He comes and gives evidence against Mr. Krajisnik. Again another feature Mr. Deronjic's evidence, and he is not the only witness to whom this applies, is that Mr. Deronjic's evidence is given when he's imminently going to be sentenced himself. There is a deal. There is no dispute about that. These deals are done all the time. There is a deal: Mr. Deronjic's cooperation with the Prosecution is potentially going to make and is supposed to make and is open to make a significant contribution to the softening of the penalty that Mr. Deronjic is going to suffer for his absolutely appalling and despicable crimes. And it could be said that, judged from many perspectives -- well, one can confidently submit this: The sentence that Mr. Deronjic received, whatever the line taken by him and his lawyers, was hardly excessive in relation to the crimes of which on his own admission he was convicted. Now, you can be a despicable war criminal like Mr. Deronjic and tell the truth. They're not logically inconsistent. But to say that his evidence in those circumstances requires care, well, that's an understatement beyond ordinary English understatement. I mentioned Mr. Okun. Of course Mr. Okun is in a totally different category from Mr. Deronjic in every single way that I have mentioned, except that, of course, one would always expect that Mr. Okun comes to tell the truth. I don't suggest that a distinguished career diplomat and gentleman such as Mr. Okun doesn't come to court to tell the truth as he sees it. Of course he does. But his direct connection with these events is, when it comes down to it, really rather slight. Although those negotiations were important, and that is the relations between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik's participation in those negotiations are an element of the Prosecution's case, and I've already dealt with that this morning, Mr. Okun, he wasn't there. He wasn't on the ground. He has no firsthand knowledge of any of the events, and he really has only that. On serious examination, slight knowledge of anything that could truly be called Mr. Krajisnik's participation, Mr. Krajisnik's role in the matters which form the subject of this indictment, it's -- the evidence is little pieces of the jigsaw. But somebody like Mr. Okun, his evidence, treated with the utmost respect as a truthful experience, good faith witness, but it really doesn't go that far. We've got witnesses like - one could almost be forgiven for thinking the case was about him at some stage rather than about Mr. Krajisnik - Mr. Davidovic. We're going to have to look again in all sorts of ways at Mr. Davidovic, but he is and, in our submission, he will remain, when the dust has settled, in the category of witnesses whose evidence will need to be treated with the greatest caution, because there are a number of witnesses, and the Defence case is that Mr. Davidovic is one of them, who have things to hide. And whenever a witness has things to hide -- Your Honour, we're not disregarding the real prospect, that that point will apply to some Defence witnesses. We don't wish to present Mr. Krajisnik's case in an unreal world, but the Prosecution have to present evidence if they wish, in the end, to see Mr. Krajisnik convicted on which he can be properly convicted. The -- a similar comment where we recognise that the point in principle may apply to Prosecution and to Defence witnesses, relates to protected witnesses. The Defence has always tried its hardest to convey to the Trial Chamber that it doesn't wish genuine protection of genuinely at-risk witnesses to be compromised in any way. That would be irresponsible, and the Trial Chamber has that heavy responsibility. And it is no part of the Defence's position to try to undermined that protection or to hamper the discharge of that responsibility. But the Defence's position has always been, as Your Honours have heard, to do its utmost to assist the Trial Chamber in keeping the protection to what is genuinely required so that as much as possible of the evidence against Mr. Krajisnik, and that will apply also to evidence given in broad terms for Mr. Krajisnik as part of his Defence, can be given in public. Not because however much we do subscribe to that as an admirable principle, it is our concern to ensure for its own sake that the public is able to follow this trial as fully as possible. That is a correct concern, a legitimate concern, and a proper part of the administration of justice. It's just not primarily our responsibility as Defence counsel. It's our responsibility to support and help that and not undermine it, but our heaviest responsibility there, consistent with our overriding duties to the Court, is to Mr. Krajisnik, which in our submission involves, and this is consistent with Mr. Krajisnik's own wishes, ensuring that as far as possible witnesses give their evidence knowing that it is being heard outside the courtroom, knowing that they are, in the fullest way that can be managed, accountable for it. Whatever the reasons and however important the protection of a witness and however admirable a witness, secret evidence, because that is what it is, secret evidence is liable to be dangerous evidence and has always to be especially carefully scrutinised, because even openly, accusations are very easy to make. Allegations are very easy to make. And they're even easier to make when you can make them in the confidence that nobody outside the direct participants in this trial will know that you're making them. We've got witnesses like Mr. Kljuic. Well, actually there's no other witness quite like Mr. Kljuic, but there's a feature of Mr. Kljuic's evidence which must be focused upon and which, in relation to other witnesses -- or raises a question which ought to be asked in relation to other witnesses. One might have thought that Mr. Kljuic, from the way in which Mr. Kljuic presented himself and the way in which Mr. Kljuic regarded himself, which came across very clearly, one might have got the impression that Mr. Kljuic's real true purpose in coming along to this Court was to assist in the search for the truth, and no doubt to this day Mr. Kljuic could convince himself that that was exactly why he came here. But Your Honours will remember that Mr. Kljuic's purpose and aim of coming here to help the Trial Chamber to see the truth ran into its limits as soon as it came into conflict with his own personal concerns about his rights of authorship to keep his documents to himself for the publication of his forthcoming book. It's not very satisfactory, is it? Mr. Kljuic's concerns about his documents and his authorship rights set against Mr. Krajisnik's concerns to have a fair trial and to be acquitted of the gravest charges that can be brought, and to have the proper prospect of leaving The Hague to go home for the rest of his life instead of spending - and nobody would suggest any other outcome if Mr. Krajisnik were convicted - instead of spending a significant part of the rest of his natural life not a free man. One really needs to look at the evidence of people like Mr. Kljuic in that light. Mr. Kljuic -- well, the school report, "this boy has performed to his own entire satisfaction throughout the whole term" has some application to Mr. Kljuic. Mr. Kljuic would be very satisfied, no doubt, with his own evidence, but the Trial Chamber should not be satisfied with Mr. Kljuic's evidence. It is deeply unsatisfactory. I'm not going to go witness through witness. I've just tried this morning to identify examples of categories or subcategories of witness where there is the strongest need to treat their evidence with great caution. There are gaps in Mr. Kljuic's evidence because he didn't produce all the material, in the end. He just didn't. The case is at a crucial watershed, of course. This case has an extraordinary tangled history anyway, even for a serious, grave, complex criminal case, criminal trial. It has an unhappily tangled history. We have the inordinately long time that Mr. Krajisnik has spent in prison awaiting the start of his trial, the suspension from practice by his own Bar of Mr. Krajisnik's previous lead counsel a few weeks before the date fixed for the beginning of the trial was a hugely disruptive event, one for which Mr. Krajisnik was not responsible in any way. It was a severe blow. It would be to any defendant in that position, and was a severe blow to Mr. Krajisnik for that to have happened. His trial was supposed to start in May 1993 -- 2003, after he had already been in prison for just over three years, and then didn't start for nearly another year, and then started. And, Your Honours, we made submissions, we made applications. They've largely been rejected, refused, but despite the rejection of various applications for more time, for adjournments, for opportunity to deal with Mr. Krajisnik's case properly, despite the rejection, it's incontrovertible, in our submission, that Mr. Krajisnik's case and Mr. Krajisnik's Defence have been prepared and have had to be prepared in something very far from satisfactory. Far from ideal, of course, but the ideal is not easily attainable anyway. But far from satisfactory circumstances. So far as the search for the truth with all the qualifications that apply, so far as search for the truth is correct, a simple label to attach to this trial, it has already not just the potential because the Defence submission is it's already happened, but it's important that the situation is not exacerbated, not aggravated for the future. It's already been seriously damaged, has the potential to be seriously damaged by that history that I've just referred to and, and this must be said, Your Honour, the completion strategy, despite -- and, Your Honour, we have heard and we understand the assurances that have continually been given, but the clear commitment by the President of this Tribunal many, many months ago to the Security Council of an end date to this trial, which has been consistently preserved, with tiny adjustments, as the end date of this trial, remains a cause for concern. There are also, and we've seen these difficulties addressed head-on recently, or quite close to head-on in decisions, in submissions made by the Defence and then the Prosecution to this Trial Chamber, and decisions that there are the extraordinarily unsatisfactory circumstances relating to the funding and resources for the Defence. Now, Your Honour, I'm not going to spend hours and hours launching into an analysis of all the directives and all that sort thing, but putting it in a nutshell, the -- they are the arrangements we've got, but the structure for dealing with a partially indigent defendant before this Tribunal, and I don't just mean this Trial Chamber but I'm concerned specifically for Mr. Krajisnik, is deeply unsatisfactory. A man is brought here, in this case Mr. Krajisnik, who sees himself, and the Defence submission is that he will ultimately be shown correctly to have seen himself as the victim of an injustice in being brought here at all. So he feels he shouldn't be here, and he's been here for five years locked up. And it's going to be six years, even on the present schedule. If Mr. Krajisnik is acquitted on all charges, he's going to have spent six years of his life in prison. And in order to have any sort of effective representation of counsel, he is expected to dig fairly deeply into his own pocket while the trial is continuing. Now, Your Honour, it's not -- there's no ruling to be sought from this Trial Chamber on the ins and outs or the rights and wrongs of that system, it is just deeply unsatisfactory. It has the potential to knock an enormous hole in the whole exercise of search for the truth. If we are going to end up with some qualified search for the truth, some seriously undermined search for the truth on the basis that the imperfections in the search of the truth, though serious, are going to be laid at Mr. Krajisnik's door, well, what the Defence has said recently, in a way, is let's know that. Let's at least know very clearly that with the way in which - and I have to say this - my predecessor's handling of the case up to April, May 2003, shortly before the trial, was clearly out of control and was clearly uncontrolled and was clearly not properly managed and controlled, it's not right that those consequences of that should now sought to be repaired at the cost of any serious impingement upon the quality of this trial and the search for the truth. And the utmost care must be taken. And it is also not right -- the United Nations has its budget. This Tribunal cannot go on to the end of this century, everybody acknowledges that, but it can't be done, and justice by this institution can't be done if corners are cut in any of the trials, let alone this enormously wide-ranging and grave charges trial against Mr. Krajisnik. It can't be done if there is any substantial failure to explore the issues and to allow the fullest presentation of Mr. Krajisnik's evidence to meet these grave charges. The -- the line has to be drawn, we submit, only at the irrelevant or the repetitive. They can overlap. There are some aspects of evidence where by the time, say, two or three witnesses have given evidence, there can be no significant addition from having another half dozen witnesses. It just doesn't add anything. That's accepted as a principle, but it has to be very carefully applied in practice. Well, repetitive equal is irrelevant in a sense. Ten witnesses each of whom individually might give relevant evidence and the last seven might simply not add anything at all. So they're in a sense either repetitive or irrelevant, but apart from that line where a witness has anything significant to add to the evidence in this case and to assist that search for the truth, then it is an impingement, it is a restriction, it is a shortfall in the administration of justice if that evidence is for any reason excluded. And if it's excluded on grounds of cost or schedules, needs to meet timetables or targets, then justice is not done. And that's not to fail to recognise that in the real world there is not perfect justice, and it's not to fail to recognise to the real world resources have to have some relevance. Of course they do. But these charges against Mr. Krajisnik are the most serious. And after spending five years, coming up to six years, in prison on these charges, the very least Mr. Krajisnik is entitled to do is not to be excluded or restricted in his legitimate wish to put forward any relevant evidence that may help him and help the Tribunal, help the Trial Chamber to see what happened to reach its verdict. The -- this is also, being a watershed in this case, this is a critical opportunity for this Trial Chamber to use Your Honours' wide-ranging, combined experience, and this is where the benefit of Your Honours' different backgrounds, although none of Your Honours are common lawyers, but you can't win them all, the combined experience and the combined benefits of Your Honours' backgrounds should make a huge positive contribution to this case. The -- it may seem a statement to the obvious, but evidence should not be made to fit into boxes. The Prosecution, legitimately, because they have an utterly different task, the Prosecution legitimately, within certain confines of what's a proper presentation, and we don't suggest those limits have been overstepped by our colleagues in this case, the Prosecution job is to present the evidence in the boxes. They make the charges, they set out the counts in the indictment, they set out the elements, and they go and get, as far as they can, the evidence to support it. That's their legitimate role. The Trial Chamber's role is to be careful not to do that. And, Your Honours, we do -- we do make the submission that at points in the Prosecution case that Your Honours were not sufficiently careful to draw that distinction and that there were points in the Prosecution case at which at the very least the impression was given that Your Honours were looking for the evidence to put in a bit of the jigsaw. If Your Honours, in the course of the Defence case -- well, I'll put it a different way. That submission on what we suggest has happened is a submission on something it won't matter at all.
